istSOS4 · OGC SensorThings API

Swagger Guide

Try istSOS4’s authentication, roles and row-level security from the Swagger page, and read the code behind every result.

KinshukGoogle Summer of Code 2026

Start here

Run Swagger

Swagger UI is the interactive documentation page that istSOS4 serves for its own API. Every endpoint is listed on it, and Try it out sends a real request from your browser and shows the response, so you can test the API without curl or Postman.

  1. Start the application

    You need Git and Docker with the Compose plugin. The example environment file is already set up for testing, so change nothing on a first run.

    Give it about a minute while the database is created and the dummy data is generated. To watch progress, run docker compose logs -f dummy_data.

  2. Open Swagger

    Go to http://localhost:8018/istsos4/v1.1/docs. You should see the istSOS4 API page, with endpoint groups such as Registration & Approval, Users and Policies.

  3. Authenticate

    Most endpoints need a token. Click the padlock button labelled Authorize at the top right and fill in the OAuth2 password form:

    • usernameadmin
    • passwordadmin, or the ISTSOS_ADMIN_PASSWORD value in your .env
    • client_id, client_secretleave both empty

    Click Authorize, then Close. The padlocks on the page now show as locked. Tokens are short-lived (five minutes by default), so if requests start returning 401 partway through, authorize again.

  4. Execute a request

    Expand an endpoint, click Try it out, fill in the parameters or the body, and click Execute. The status code, body and headers appear directly below. Always send requests this way. The Request URL link and the browser address bar can only send GET, so a PATCH or POST opened there fails with a 404 or 405 that looks like a bug and is not one.

  5. What you should see

    • 200POST /Login with the admin credentials returns a bearer access_token.
    • 401A request to /Datastreams without a token answers {"detail": "Not authenticated"}.
    • 401A signed-in viewer calling GET /Users gets {"message": "Insufficient privileges."}.

    These are the exact responses recorded in tests A2, C2 and A6. From here, the test list shows what to try next.

S0SQLNetwork / Datastream / Observation counts#

Read the Networks, their Datastream and Observation counts, and the feature flags the API is running with.

Expected
Two Networks that each own Datastreams; AUTHORIZATION=1 and NETWORK=1.
Actual
acsot: 10 datastreams / 20160 obs · psos: 10 / 20160 · AUTHORIZATION=1 NETWORK=1 ANONYMOUS_VIEWER=0 VERSIONING=1 REDIS=0
Run in SwaggerOpen Swagger
  1. Check .env: AUTHORIZATION=1, NETWORK=1, ANONYMOUS_VIEWER=0. Restart the api container after changing them.
  2. Run the query below in the database container and note the two Network names and counts. The dummy-data generator picks two names at random from psos, acsot, defmin on every fresh build, so later steps say “your Network”.

How it works. The seed generator creates the Networks, assigns every Datastream to one of them, and skips itself when data already exists, so counts stay stable across restarts.

Inputs. The running database and the API container's environment.

Behaviour. Scoping later in the guide is expressed against these names and counts.

What the test verifies. At least two Networks hold Datastreams, and auth plus Network scoping are switched on in the API that is being tested.

Depends on. NETWORK=1 creates the Network table and Datastream.network_id; without it there is nothing to scope by.

Part A · 12 tests

Local account lifecycle

Registration through deactivation for a password account: pending, approved, re-scoped, re-keyed, logged out, rejected, deactivated.

/

A1POST/Register#

Self-registration creates a pending account that holds the requested role and Network as a preference, not a grant.

Expected
201 — status: pending, with the new id
Actual
201 · status=pending · id=17
Run in SwaggerOpen Swagger
  1. Registration & Approval → POST /Register → Try it out.
  2. Use one of your Network names for dataset_id (optional; omit it for unscoped access). requested_role is required. Both are only a preference: the admin decides the real grant.
  3. Execute and note the returned id.

How it works. The handler bcrypt-hashes the password off the event loop, then inserts the row with role='pending' and status='pending' and writes an audit event in the same transaction. A previously rejected username is re-used by updating that row instead of inserting.

Inputs. A validated RestrictedRegistrationRequest: username rules, password strength and an assignable requested_role are enforced by the Pydantic model before the handler runs.

Behaviour. No PostgreSQL role is created. pending maps to no group role, so the account can do nothing yet.

What the test verifies. 201 with status: pending and an id.

Depends on. Migrations 002 (password, status), 005 (dataset_id), 007 (requested_role) and 003 (AuditLog).

A2POST/Login#

Password login for the bootstrap administrator returns a signed JWT that Swagger keeps in the padlock.

Expected
200 — access_token, token_type: bearer
Actual
200 · bearer token issued for admin
Run in SwaggerOpen Swagger
  1. Click Authorize (padlock, top right).
  2. Under OAuth2PasswordBearer enter admin and your ISTSOS_ADMIN_PASSWORD. Leave client_id and client_secret empty.
  3. Authorize → Close.

How it works. /Login calls authenticate_user, which reads the user row and verifies the bcrypt hash in a worker thread. On success it signs a JWT carrying only sub and role.

Inputs. Form fields username and password (OAuth2 password flow).

Behaviour. Rejected and deactivated accounts are refused even with the right password; a pending account gets 403 instead of a token.

What the test verifies. 200 and a bearer token for admin.

Depends on. SECRET_KEY, ALGORITHM and ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRE_MINUTES from the environment.

A3GET/Users#

The admin user list shows the applicant as pending, with no effective role and never the password hash.

Expected
200 — role: null, status: pending, requested values stored
Actual
200 · role=null · status=pending · dataset_id=acsot · requested_role=viewer
Run in SwaggerOpen Swagger
  1. Users → GET /Users → Try it out → Execute.
  2. Find the new row.

How it works. An administrator-only query returns every row ordered by id. The password column is stripped before serialising, and the internal pending role sentinel is reported as null.

Inputs. An administrator token.

Behaviour. Ordering by primary key keeps positions stable: an UPDATE writes a new row version elsewhere in the heap.

What the test verifies. role: null, status: pending, the requested Network and role, no password key, and ascending ids.

Depends on. set_role() switches to the administrator group role for the read.

A4PATCH/Users/{target_user_id}/policy-approval#

An administrator grants a role (defaulting to the requested one) and a Network scope, which must name an existing Network.

Expected
200 — granted_role: viewer, status becomes active
Actual
200 · granted_role=viewer · dataset_id=acsot · status=active
Run in SwaggerOpen Swagger
  1. Registration & Approval → PATCH /Users/{target_user_id}/policy-approval.
  2. target_user_id: the id from A1. role is optional and falls back to requested_role.

How it works. Inside one transaction the handler locks the pending row, resolves the role, validates dataset_id against the Network table, activates the account and writes an ADMIN_APPROVAL audit event.

Inputs. AdminApprovalRequest with optional role and dataset_id.

Behaviour. A rejected applicant cannot be approved directly (400); an unknown Network name is refused (400) so a scope can never silently match nothing.

What the test verifies. 200 with granted_role: viewer, and the row reads role: viewer, status: active.

Depends on. NETWORK=1 enables the Network-name check.

A5POST/Login#

Once active, the account logs in through the same bcrypt path and receives its own token.

Expected
200 — a token for the approved user
Actual
200 · token issued for the approved user
Run in SwaggerOpen Swagger
  1. Click Authorize again and log in as demo_alice / Str0ng!Pass1.
  2. This replaces the admin token; every call now runs as her.

How it works. The token carries only the username and role. Nothing about the Network scope is in the token; it is looked up per request.

Inputs. The username and password from A1.

Behaviour. Because role and status are re-read on every request, the token never holds stale privileges.

What the test verifies. 200 and a token.

Depends on. The approval in A4; before it, /Login answers 403 Account is pending administrator approval.

A6GET/Users#

A viewer asking for the user list is refused.

Expected
401 — {"message": "Insufficient privileges."}
Actual
401 · {"message": "Insufficient privileges."}
Run in SwaggerOpen Swagger
  1. Still authorized as demo_alice: Users → GET /Users → Execute.

How it works. The handler raises InsufficientPrivilegeError for any caller whose live role is not administrator; the error is mapped to 401 with an explicit message.

Inputs. The viewer's token.

Behaviour. Beyond this check, the user group role also has SELECT on "User" revoked, so the data is protected at the database even if the check were removed.

What the test verifies. 401 with Insufficient privileges.

Depends on. get_current_user supplies the live role.

A7POST/Refresh#

Exchanges a still-valid token for a fresh one with a new expiry.

Expected
200 — a new access_token
Actual
200 · fresh access_token, accepted on the next call
Run in SwaggerOpen Swagger
  1. Authentication → POST /Refresh → Try it out → Execute. No body; the token is read from the padlock.

How it works. The handler reads the bearer header itself, refuses a token already on the Redis deny-list, decodes it, and signs a new one with the same sub and role. With REDIS=1 the old token is added to the deny-list.

Inputs. Authorization: Bearer <token>.

Behaviour. A malformed header is 400, an undecodable token is 400, a revoked one is 401.

What the test verifies. 200 and a new token that the next call accepts.

Depends on. Redis only for revoking the old token.

PreviousA6 Prove the RBAC boundaryNextA8 Change the role
A8PATCH/Users/{user_id}/role#

An administrator re-assigns an active user's role; the change applies on that user's very next request.

Expected
204 — GET /Users shows role: editor
Actual
204 · role is now editor
Run in SwaggerOpen Swagger
  1. Authorize back as admin.
  2. Users → PATCH /Users/{user_id}/role, user_id from A1.
  3. The same endpoint accepts dataset to re-scope an active user; "" clears it.

How it works. One UPDATE of the role column. No PostgreSQL role is created, altered or granted: the next request's set_role() simply maps the new value to its group role.

Inputs. RoleUpdateRequest with role and/or dataset (at least one required).

Behaviour. Pending users must be activated instead (400); demoting the last administrator is refused (409); an unknown Network is refused (400).

What the test verifies. 204 and the new role in the user list.

Depends on. get_current_user re-reading role live, so no token rotation is needed.

PreviousA7 Refresh the tokenNextA9 Change the password
A9PATCH/Users/{user_id}/password#

A local user changes their own password after proving the current one.

Expected
204 — old password refused, new password accepted
Actual
204 · old password → 401 · new password → 200
Run in SwaggerOpen Swagger
  1. Authorize as demo_alice.
  2. Users → PATCH /Users/{user_id}/password, user_id from A1.
  3. Then try Authorize with the old password (fails) and the new one (works).

How it works. The endpoint allows only the account owner or an administrator. The CRUD layer verifies the current password against the stored bcrypt hash and writes a new hash.

Inputs. PasswordUpdateRequest; new_password must meet the strength rules.

Behaviour. External identities have no local password and get 400; a wrong current password is 401.

What the test verifies. 204, then /Login with the old password is 401 and with the new one 200.

Depends on. Migration 002 (password column).

PreviousA8 Change the roleNextA10 Log out
A10POST/Logout#

Logout is acknowledged; the token is revoked only when Redis is enabled.

Expected
200 — {"message": "Successfully logged out"}
Actual
200 · REDIS=0: acknowledged, token not revoked until it expires
Run in SwaggerOpen Swagger
  1. As demo_alice: Authentication → POST /Logout → Execute.
  2. With REDIS=1, any further call with the same token returns 401 Token has been revoked. With REDIS=0 (the default) the token keeps working until it expires.
  3. Tokens have no unique id: a login within the same second as a logout returns the same, revoked token. Wait a second.

How it works. The handler decodes the token for its expiry and, when REDIS=1, stores it in Redis with a TTL that ends exactly when the token would have expired. get_current_user and /Refresh consult that list first.

Inputs. Authorization: Bearer <token>.

Behaviour. Without Redis there is no deny-list, so the call is an acknowledgement only. Deactivation (A12) is the revocation path that works regardless.

What the test verifies. 200 and the documented behaviour for the running REDIS setting.

Depends on. REDIS and the Redis container.

A11PATCH/Users/{target_user_id}/reject#

A rejected applicant cannot log in, but may register again under the same username.

Expected
200 — status: rejected; re-registering returns 201 and resets to pending
Actual
200 reject · login 401 · re-apply 201 · status back to pending
Run in SwaggerOpen Swagger
  1. Register a second applicant (demo_bob) as in A1.
  2. As admin: PATCH /Users/{target_user_id}/reject with the new id.
  3. Log in as demo_bob (401), then repeat A1 with the same username (201).

How it works. Rejection flips only status to rejected for a pending row and records an ADMIN_REJECTION audit event. Registration treats a rejected row as reusable and updates it back to pending instead of raising a username conflict.

Inputs. RejectRequest with an optional reason.

Behaviour. authenticate_user refuses a rejected account with a message asking the applicant to re-register.

What the test verifies. 200, role: null and status: rejected, login 401, re-register 201, status back to pending.

Depends on. Migration 004 extends the AuditLog action constraint with ADMIN_REJECTION.

A12DELETE/Users#

Deactivation keeps the row and its audit history, and cuts off a still-valid token on its next use.

Expected
200 — login with the valid password now fails
Actual
200 · status=deleted · login with the valid password → 401
Run in SwaggerOpen Swagger
  1. Authorize as admin.
  2. Users → DELETE /Users, query user=demo_alice.
  3. Then try logging in as her with the current password.

How it works. The endpoint sets status='deleted' rather than deleting: the append-only AuditLog references users and must stay intact. Both login and get_current_user refuse a deleted account.

Inputs. Query parameter user (validated username).

Behaviour. Deactivating yourself is refused (400), an unknown user is 404, deactivating twice is 409.

What the test verifies. 200, status: deleted, and login with the valid password is 401.

Depends on. Nothing beyond the database; works with REDIS=0.

Part B · 4 tests

External (OIDC) authentication

The same pending → approve → active lifecycle for an identity that signs in through an OpenID provider and has no local password.

/

B1GET/auth/{provider}/login#

The login route stores the requested Network and role in the server session and redirects to the provider.

Expected
302 — redirect to the provider's authorize page
Actual
302 → provider /authorize (state + nonce set)
Run in SwaggerOpen Swagger
  1. Open a new browser tab (Swagger's Try it out cannot follow a cross-origin redirect):
  2. http://localhost:8018/istsos4/v1.1/auth/google/login?dataset_id=<your Network>&requested_role=viewer
  3. Swap google for microsoft, github or orcid. Never reload a callback tab: the code is single-use.

How it works. A redirect has no body, so dataset_id and requested_role are kept in the signed server session until the callback. Authlib builds the authorize URL with state (CSRF) and nonce (replay protection).

Inputs. Path provider, optional dataset_id and requested_role (validated against assignable roles).

Behaviour. Only providers with both client id and secret configured are registered; others are 404 (B4).

What the test verifies. 302 to the provider's /authorize with state and nonce.

Depends on. *_CLIENT_ID / *_CLIENT_SECRET. The automated run uses the bundled fake OpenID provider.

PreviousA12 Deactivate the accountNextB2 Complete the provider consent
B2GET/auth/{provider}/callback#

The callback verifies the provider's token and creates a pending account from the verified claims.

Expected
202 — Registration submitted via google; account pending
Actual
202 · Registration submitted via google · account pending
Run in SwaggerOpen Swagger
  1. Sign in on the provider's own page and approve.
  2. Already signed in? The provider may skip straight back; use a private window to see the full form.

How it works. authorize_access_token exchanges the code on the back channel and verifies the RS256 id_token (signature against JWKS, iss, aud, exp, nonce). Claims are normalised per provider, the username sanitised, and an unknown (provider, sub) becomes a pending row with an audit event.

Inputs. code and state from the provider redirect.

Behaviour. An unknown identity is never granted access automatically. The identity key is (auth_provider, external_sub_id), not the mutable email.

What the test verifies. 202 with the pending message.

Depends on. The provider's discovery document and JWKS.

PreviousB1 Start the external loginNextB3 Activate the external identity
B3POST/Users/{user_id}/activate#

An administrator activates the pending identity; the next sign-in returns a token that behaves like a local one.

Expected
200 — activated with role 'viewer'; the next callback returns a token
Actual
200 activate · callback 200 + token · sees 10 psos datastreams
Run in SwaggerOpen Swagger
  1. As admin, GET /Users and find the row with auth_provider: "google" and status: "pending".
  2. POST /Users/{user_id}/activate with {} to accept the requested role, or {"role": "viewer"}.
  3. Open the B1 URL again: the callback now returns an access_token.
  4. In Swagger, Authorize → BearerAuth and paste it.

How it works. Activation moves a pending row to its role (the requested one unless overridden), optionally re-scopes it, and writes an audit event. The callback then finds an active (provider, sub) and signs the same kind of JWT as /Login.

Inputs. Optional role and dataset in the body.

Behaviour. Retrying the login while pending returns 202 every time; activation is the only way out. External accounts have password IS NULL.

What the test verifies. 200, a token on the second callback, and that token sees exactly its Network's Datastreams.

Depends on. B2's pending row.

B4GET/auth/eduid/login#

A provider without credentials is not registered, and its routes answer 404.

Expected
404 — names the unconfigured provider
Actual
404 for an unconfigured provider (eduid)
Run in SwaggerOpen Swagger
  1. Google, GitHub: work with their credentials set.
  2. Microsoft: registered for organisational accounts only; personal Outlook accounts fail at Microsoft's consent screen.
  3. ORCID: points at the ORCID sandbox; use a sandbox account.
  4. SWITCH edu-ID: not configured here, so /auth/eduid/login is 404.

How it works. At import time each provider registers only if both its client id and secret are non-empty. _client_for rejects any other name.

Inputs. The provider path parameter.

Behaviour. Nothing is half-configured: an unset provider fails fast with 404 instead of at the redirect.

What the test verifies. 404 for eduid, with the provider named in the error.

Depends on. Environment variables only.

C

Part C · 10 tests

Data visibility and Network scoping

What each role can read and change once authenticated, enforced by PostgreSQL row-level security rather than by the API.

/

C1SQLpg_policies#

Every role's access comes from a fixed set of row-level-security policies written once for the deployment.

Expected
All rbac_* policies present; RLS enabled on the scoped tables
Actual
42 rbac_* policies · RLS on 9 tables
Run in SwaggerOpen Swagger
  1. Read the matrix below, then Policies → GET /Policies as admin to see the installed policies by name.

How it works. Migration 006 generates one SELECT policy per group role and table, plus write policies per role. Several application roles share a group role (viewer, editor and custom all run as user), so predicates tell them apart through current_app_user_role().

Inputs. custom.network at migration time decides whether the Network predicates are generated.

Behaviour. Policies are static: no policy is ever created per user for the built-in roles. The number of PostgreSQL roles stays fixed at seven no matter how many users exist.

What the test verifies. The expected policy names exist and RLS is enabled on the scoped tables.

Depends on. set_role() on every request, and the helper functions.

Depends on. ANONYMOUS_VIEWER=0.

C3GET/Datastreams#

Two users on the same PostgreSQL role see different rows, decided by their Network grant.

Expected
200 — exactly the Datastreams of the viewer's Network; admin sees all
Actual
viewer(acsot) sees 10 · admin sees 20
Run in SwaggerOpen Swagger
  1. Authorize as a viewer approved with a Network (A4).
  2. GET /Datastreams, $top 50 → Execute.
  3. Repeat as admin and compare.

How it works. The read runs in a transaction that first calls set_role(): SET LOCAL ROLE "user" plus app.current_user_id. The Datastream SELECT policy then keeps rows whose network_id equals current_app_user_network_id(), which resolves the caller's Network name to an id.

Inputs. The viewer's token; the Network name stored on their row.

Behaviour. A Network name that matches nothing yields no rows (fail-closed). An unscoped viewer (dataset_id null) sees every Network.

What the test verifies. The viewer's ids equal the Network's ids from Setup; admin sees at least both Networks.

Depends on. NETWORK=1; the administrator group owns the tables and bypasses RLS.

C4PATCH/Datastreams({datastream_id})#

The row is visible, but no write policy matches a viewer, so the update affects nothing and is reported as 403.

Expected
403 — Insufficient privileges to update this Datastream.
Actual
403 · Insufficient privileges to update this Datastream.
Run in SwaggerOpen Swagger
  1. As the viewer: PATCH /Datastreams({datastream_id}) with one of their own ids.
  2. Header commit-message: demo.

How it works. The existence probe succeeds because SELECT is allowed. The UPDATE then matches zero rows under RLS, update_entity returns False, and the handler turns that into an explicit 403 instead of a silent 200.

Inputs. Viewer token, a visible Datastream id, a JSON patch body.

Behaviour. PostgreSQL does not raise on an UPDATE filtered away by RLS; checking the affected row is what makes the refusal visible.

What the test verifies. 403 with the explicit message.

Depends on. Only editor has a write policy on Datastream in the user group.

Things, Sensors, Locations and the other reference tables are shared: any authenticated role reads all of them.

  1. Still as the viewer: Things → GET /Things, $count true → Execute.

How it works. In the read-policy generator, only Datastream and Observation receive a Network predicate; every other table gets TRUE.

Inputs. Viewer token.

Behaviour. Deliberate scope: a Thing or Sensor can be referenced by Datastreams in several Networks, so it has no single owning Network.

What the test verifies. The viewer's count equals the table's full count.

Depends on. Documented as a known limitation in the final report.

C6POST/Datastreams#

A Network-scoped editor can create a Datastream that belongs to its own Network.

Expected

  2. POST /Datastreams, header commit-message: editor create test.
  3. Use existing Thing / Sensor / ObservedProperty ids and your own Network's id.

How it works. The insert runs as the user group role; the editor write policy's WITH CHECK accepts the new row because its network_id equals the caller's Network.

Inputs. Editor token, commit message, the Datastream payload.

Behaviour. With VERSIONING=1 the write is attached to a commit authored by the caller.

What the test verifies. 201 and a location header.

Depends on. The editor write policy.

PreviousC5 Reference tables are not Network-scopedNextC7 An editor is blocked outside its Network
C7POST/Datastreams · PATCH /Datastreams({id})#

Creating into another Network fails the policy check; another Network's rows look like they do not exist.

Expected
POST → 403 Insufficient privileges. · PATCH → 404 Datastream not found.
Actual
POST into other Network → 403 · PATCH other Network's row → 404
Run in SwaggerOpen Swagger
  1. Repeat C6 with the other Network's id → 403.
  2. PATCH /Datastreams({datastream_id}) on a row of the other Network → 404.

How it works. The INSERT violates the policy's WITH CHECK, PostgreSQL raises InsufficientPrivilegeError, and a global handler maps it to 403. For the PATCH, the existence probe is a SELECT that RLS already filters, so the row is simply not found.

Inputs. Editor token and a Network or row outside its scope.

Behaviour. RLS hides out-of-scope rows entirely; there is no “exists but forbidden” signal to leak their existence.

What the test verifies. 403 for the insert and 404 for the update.

Depends on. Registered exception handlers in the app.

C8GET/Observations?$count=true#

Observation has no Network column; its scope flows down from its parent Datastream.

Expected
200 — @iot.count equals the viewer's Network's observations
Actual
200 · @iot.count=20160 (whole table: 40320)
Run in SwaggerOpen Swagger
  1. As the scoped viewer: GET /Observations, $count true, $top 0 → Execute.

How it works. The Observation policy tests datastream_id = ANY(current_app_user_datastream_ids()). A function returning an array is used instead of an IN (SELECT …) subquery because TimescaleDB's SkipScan aborts on the subplan a subquery creates, which made $count fail with a 500.

Inputs. Viewer token, $count=true.

Behaviour. An unknown Network yields an empty array, never NULL, so the predicate stays fail-closed.

What the test verifies. The count equals the Setup count for the viewer's Network, not the whole table.

Depends on. Observation is a TimescaleDB hypertable.

C9GET/Policies · /Commits#

Neither table has a per-user or per-Network column, so both are restricted outright.

Expected
viewer 401 · admin 200 (both endpoints)
Actual
Policies 401/200 · Commits 401/200 (viewer/admin)
Run in SwaggerOpen Swagger
  1. As the viewer: GET /Policies, then GET /Commits → 401.
  2. As admin: both → 200.
  3. GET /Commits only exists with VERSIONING=1.

How it works. Both handlers raise InsufficientPrivilegeError for any non-administrator before building a query. The Commits router is only mounted when versioning is on.

Inputs. A token.

Behaviour. Filtering would be meaningless: policies and commits describe the whole deployment.

What the test verifies. 401 for a viewer and 200 for admin on both.

Depends on. VERSIONING=1 for Commits.

PreviousC8 Observation counts follow the Network scopeNextC10 An external identity behaves identically
C10GET/Datastreams · /Observations · PATCH#

A Google-authenticated viewer and a local viewer in the same Network get the same answers.

Expected
Identical counts, 403 on own rows, 404 on other rows
Actual
identical on datastreams, observation count, 403 own, 404 other
Run in SwaggerOpen Swagger
  1. Complete B1–B3 with a dataset_id, paste the token into BearerAuth, and repeat C3, C4 and C8.

How it works. Nothing downstream reads auth_provider: get_current_user returns role and status, set_role() maps the role, and policies read the Network grant. Both identity types therefore take the same path.

Inputs. The external token from B3 and a local viewer in the same Network.

Behaviour. The only designed difference is that external identities cannot set a local password.

What the test verifies. Datastream ids, observation count and both PATCH outcomes are equal.

Depends on. B3. A scripted version covers six roles × 26 operations (run_auth_parity.py).

Part D · 5 tests

The custom role

A role with no standing grant: an administrator writes per-user RLS rules, so read and write scope can differ row by row.

/

D1POST/Users#

The custom role starts with zero access: no standing policy matches it.

Expected
201 — the new user's GET /Datastreams returns value: []
Actual
201 · GET /Datastreams → value: []
Run in SwaggerOpen Swagger
  1. As admin: Users → POST /Users.
  2. Authorize as demo_custom and run GET /Datastreams.

How it works. custom maps to the user group role, but every user-group read policy is gated on current_app_user_role() <> 'custom', so none of them applies.

Inputs. Username, password, role.

Behaviour. Admin-created accounts are active immediately; the password is validated and bcrypt-hashed.

What the test verifies. 201 and an empty Datastream list for the new user.

Depends on. The read-policy generator's custom gate.

D2POST/Policies#

One call creates one RLS policy per operation, so read and write scope can differ for the same user.

Expected
201 — <name>_datastream_select and _update created
Actual
201 · demo_custom_mixed_b7d78_datastream_select + _update created
Run in SwaggerOpen Swagger
  1. As admin: Policies → POST /Policies.
  2. Pick two Datastream ids from Setup as <A> and <B>.
  3. A row must be in select to be writable at all: every write first checks existence with an RLS-scoped SELECT. Make select a superset of the other operations.

How it works. create_policies resolves the users (all must have role custom), then emits CREATE POLICY <name>_<table>_<op> … TO "user" whose predicate is current_app_user_id() = ANY(<ids>) AND (<condition>). Identifiers are quoted and conditions are screened for unsafe tokens.

Inputs. users, name, and permissions.policy keyed by table then operation.

Behaviour. Built-in role types return 200 without creating anything; they are already covered by static policies. A duplicate name is 409.

What the test verifies. 201 and both policy names present in GET /Policies.

Depends on. current_app_user_id() from the session helpers.

D3GETPATCH/Datastreams#

The custom user reads both granted rows, writes only one, and cannot see anything else.

Expected
sees [A, B] · PATCH A 403 · PATCH B 200 · other id 404
Actual
sees [5, 6] · PATCH read-only 403 · granted 200 · other 404
Run in SwaggerOpen Swagger
  1. As demo_custom: GET /Datastreams → exactly <A> and <B>.
  2. PATCH /Datastreams(<A>) → 403, PATCH /Datastreams(<B>) → 200.
  3. Open /Datastreams(<other id>) in a new tab → 404.

How it works. <A> passes the SELECT policy but not the UPDATE one, so the update affects no row (403). <B> passes both. Any other id fails the SELECT policy, so the existence probe reports it as not found.

Inputs. The custom user's token.

Behaviour. Separate policies per operation are what make the split possible.

What the test verifies. The visible set, both PATCH outcomes and the 404.

Depends on. D2's policies.

Background

Reference

/

OverviewWhat was tested, how, and against what

istSOS4 is an open-source server for the OGC SensorThings API, which stores sensor observations. When authentication is switched on, every request is decided by two things: who is asking, and which Network the data belongs to. A wrong decision either leaks observations or locks out a legitimate user.

This guide exercises that decision layer end to end. All 32 tests ran against a live deployment, and each records what it expected, what came back, and which lines of source produced the result. A claim about access control can therefore be checked against both the traffic and the code.

What the tests cover

  • Setup: what the deployment contains before anything is asserted.
  • Part A: the life of a local account, from registration to deactivation.
  • Part B: signing in through an external OpenID provider.
  • Part C: what each role can see and change, enforced by PostgreSQL row-level security.
  • Part D: a custom role whose access is granted row by row.

PrerequisitesWhat to have installed before you start
  • Git, to clone the repository.
  • Docker with the Compose plugin, so that docker compose works. Every image is built from the repository; nothing is pulled except base images.
  • Free ports. The API answers on 8018 and PostgreSQL is published on 45432. Both can be changed in .env (EXTERNAL_PORT, POSTGRES_EXTERNAL_PORT).
  • A modern browser for Swagger UI.
  • Optional, for Part B: a client id and secret from Google, GitHub, Microsoft, ORCID or SWITCH edu-ID if you want to complete a real external sign-in. Without them the API reports that provider as unconfigured, which is itself tested in B4.

The admin password is whatever ISTSOS_ADMIN_PASSWORD is set to in your .env. If you are not sure what the running container uses, ask it:

SetupThe settings that matter, and how to reset

.env.example ships with the right values for testing. These are the ones the tests depend on:

SettingValueWhy it matters
AUTHORIZATION1Authentication, roles and row-level security are only active when this is 1.
NETWORK1Creates the Network table and Datastream.network_id. Without it there is nothing to scope by.
ANONYMOUS_VIEWER0Anonymous requests are refused (test C2).
VERSIONING1Keeps the edit history behind GET /Commits.
DUMMY_DATA1Generates the sample Networks and Datastreams that the scoping tests act on.
REDIS0With 0, POST /Logout succeeds but the token keeps working until it expires. Set 1 to revoke it for real.

Do not set AUTHORIZATION or NETWORK back to 0, or none of the features in this guide are active.

Make logout actually revoke

Set REDIS=1 in .env, then restart only the API. A logged-out token is then rejected with 401 "Token has been revoked". Tokens carry no unique id, so if you log in again within the same second as a logout you receive the same, still-revoked token. Wait a second.

Start again from a clean database

Re-running docker compose up is safe, because the dummy-data generator skips itself when data exists. To wipe everything:

AuthenticationAccounts, roles, tokens and external sign-in

The life of a local account

Nobody gets access by registering. An application is held as pending, an administrator reviews it, and only approval turns it into a working account with a role.

  1. POST /Register creates a pending account (A1).
  2. An administrator lists the queue with GET /Users (A3).
  3. PATCH /Users/{target_user_id}/policy-approval grants the role (A4).
  4. The user signs in with POST /Login and receives a bearer token (A5).
  5. The token can be renewed with POST /Refresh (A7) and ended with POST /Logout (A10).

Roles

RoleWhat it can doTests
pendingNothing yet. No database role is created.A1
viewerReads only the Datastreams and Observations of its own Network. Cannot write, even there.C3 C4 C8
editorCreates and updates inside its own Network. Blocked outside it.C6 C7
customStarts with no access. An administrator grants rules per user, so read and write can differ row by row.D1 D3
adminSees every Network, and alone reads Policies and Commits.C9

Tokens

Signing in returns a bearer token. Swagger’s Authorize button attaches it to every request for you. Tokens expire after five minutes by default (ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRE_MINUTES).

External sign-in

Google, Microsoft, GitHub, ORCID and SWITCH edu-ID are supported. A provider only registers when both its client id and secret are set, so leaving a pair empty disables just that provider. The redirect URI to register with the provider is:

An external identity has no local password. It follows the same pending, approved, active lifecycle (Part B), and once active it behaves exactly like a local account with the same role (C10).

Implementation detailsWhere the rules live, and an index of the source

The rules are split across two layers, and the tests are written to prove which layer decides what.

The API layer
FastAPI endpoints validate input with Pydantic models, check the token and the caller’s role, and answer 401 or 403. Registration, login, approval and role changes live here, and changes such as registration write an append-only audit row in the same transaction.
The database layer
Which rows a signed-in user can read or write is decided by PostgreSQL row-level security, not by the API. The recorded run had 42 rbac_* policies with row-level security on 9 tables (C1). That is why a viewer’s query for another Network’s row returns 404: the row does not exist for that user at all.

TroubleshootingThe problems people actually hit
Authorize answers 401
The username or password is wrong. Copy the password exactly, with no quotes and no trailing space. If you are unsure of it, read it from the container as shown under Prerequisites.
Authorize fails for a confusing reason
Something was typed into client_secret. The app does not use client_id or client_secret; leave both empty.
Requests turn into 401 halfway through
The token expired. Click Authorize again.
A PATCH, POST or DELETE gives 404 or 405 in a new tab
You opened the endpoint’s URL in the browser, which sends GET. Send it with Try it out and Execute inside Swagger.
Lists come back empty, or the page will not load
The stack may still be starting. Follow docker compose logs -f dummy_data until the generator finishes.
Logout succeeds but the token still works
REDIS is 0. See Setup to turn revocation on.
Registration says the username is taken
In the tested build, deactivating a user keeps the row and its username, so a name cannot be reused. Add a suffix such as demo_alice_2 for each run.
An external login answers 404
That provider has no client id and secret configured. Set both in .env and restart the API.
Auth features seem to be switched off
Check that AUTHORIZATION and NETWORK are both 1 in .env, then run docker compose up -d --build.
Additional notesCleaning up, provenance and links

Cleaning up after a run

Authorize as admin, then call DELETE /Users?user=<username> for each account you created. This deactivates the account rather than removing it: the row and its username stay, and the audit trail is kept. It keeps GET /Users tidy but does not free the username.

How this guide is made

It is generated from two files in the istSOS4 repository: catalog.py, which maps each test to the source it exercises, and checks.py, which holds the executable checks. Code excerpts are read from the working tree at build time, and a reference that no longer resolves fails the build. The page you are reading is rebuilt from that report by tools/build.py in this repository.
